Learning Objectives
Identify risk factors and approaches for the treatment of patients with periprosthetic femur or
acetabulum fractures.
Discuss the classification of periprosthetic femur and acetabulum fractures and the subtypes
of each fracture.
Explain how fracture morphology may dictate management.
Recognize the extent of treatment options and understand the principles of fixation that guide
the management of periprosthetic femur and acetabulum fractures.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
The incidence of intraoperative periprosthetic femur fractures is 1.7% for primary total hip
arthroplasty (THA) and as high as 12.3% for revision THA.1,2
The incidence of postoperative periprosthetic femur fractures at more than 20 years is 3.5%
for primary THA and 11% for revision THA.1,2

Epidemiology
Periprosthetic fractures are one of the most common complications after a THA;
however, the literature reporting the incidence is variable because of different study
characteristics, such as patient population, mode of fixation, and period over which
patients are followed1-6
Mechanism of Injury
Trauma is the most cited cause of periprosthetic femur fractures.

Mechanism of Injury
Most periprosthetic femur fractures result from low-energy mechanisms of injury, such
as a fall from standing height. A smaller percentage of reported fractures result from
higher energy mechanisms of injury. As the number of individuals with osteoporotic
bone, osteolysis, and loosening who undergo THA increases, the incidence of fracture
secondary to low-energy trauma increases. Conversely, as the indications for THA
expand, younger, more active patients who undergo THA may be more susceptible to
higher energy trauma. High-energy trauma ultimately accounts for less than 10% of
periprosthetic femur fractures.5,7

Risk Factors and Etiology
Female sex
Increasing age
Noncemented stems
Revision THA
Loosening and osteolysis
Inflammatory arthropathies may compound osteopenia.6
Paget disease also may alter bone morphology and its’ mechanical properties, which may
make patients more susceptible to periprosthetic fracture.
Surgical technique

Risk Factors and Etiology
Women sustain a higher reported percentage of periprosthetic fractures, which may be
associated with osteoporosis.4,6,8
Elderly patients, particularly those older than 70 years, should be counseled on the
increased risk of periprosthetic fracture in osteoporotic bone, especially given the
expanding aging population with a greater life expectancy.9
Various biomechanical strategies are used with noncemented, proximally fit, tapered
femoral stems to achieve fixation and attain stability within the metaphysis. They
promote osseointegration and are favored in younger, more active patients; however,
increased stress on the proximal femur may lead to fracture in the early postoperative
period, and stress shielding and osteolysis may lead to an increased risk of fracture in
the late postoperative period.10,11
Revision THA may be associated with increased bone loss, challenging fixation, wear
debris, and osteolysis, which contribute to an increased rate of fracture. The mean time
between surgical management and fracture is 7.4 years after a primary THA, 3.9 years
after one revision THA procedure, 3.8 years after two revision THA procedures, and 2.3
years after three revision THA procedures.4

Compared with well-fixed stems, loose stems are associated with a 60% reduction in
torque to failure.12 Patients with a loose stem may sustain a fracture at loads that are
more commonly associated with activities of daily living rather than from high- or low-
energy trauma. Studies have shown that as many as 27% of patients with a
periprosthetic femur fracture had evidence of loosening preoperatively.5
Surgical risk factors that decrease bone strength or bone stock, such as drill holes, stress
risers from adjacent hardware, cortical perforations from cement removal, or osteolytic
lesions, increase the risk of periprosthetic femur fractures.6 Techniques that transmit
forces to the tip of the stem, such as noncemented press-fit stems versus cemented
technique may lead to a higher rate of periprosthetic fractures.13 In addition, although
rarely performed, impaction grafting may be used to manage areas of comminution by
reconstituting metaphyseal bone stock; however, this increases the risk of fracture.
Prophylactic cerclage wires and cortical onlay strut allografts are recommended to
reduce this risk.14,15
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Functional status and symptoms prior to injury must be elicited.
History of pain in the thigh or start-up pain may indicate loosening prior to injury.
A thorough review of medical records may help establish preexisting symptoms. It also may
help identify the previous surgical approach and existing implants, which may guide
preoperative planning.
A history of delayed wound healing, drainage, or systemic signs of infection may prompt an
infectious workup.
Physical Examination
Although a physical examination is limited by pain, surgeons must assess the condition of the
skin, the location of scars, and leg-length discrepancies.
Imaging Studies

Radiography
A minimum of two full-length radiographic views (AP and lateral) of the femur should be
obtained to identify the type and extent of the fracture. These should be assessed for cortical
perforations, longitudinal splits, displaced fracture fragments, comminution, and signs of
component instability. Fracture lines also may be obscured by a metallic component.14
CT and MRI
Routine use of advanced imaging modalities, such as ultrasonography, CT, and MRI, is not
warranted; however, they may be helpful if fractures are minimally displaced and difficult to
visualize. These studies may help identify fracture morphology and aid in preoperative
planning. They also may aid in assessment of component fixation via evaluation of bone-
implant surface integration. Advanced imaging studies, such as MRIs and CT scans, may be
warranted if patients are unable to ambulate and have inconclusive or negative radiographs.15
Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy typically is not necessary but may help identify late fractures not observed
on plain radiographs; however, bone scans may show areas of increased uptake in the
absence of fracture for 1 to 2 years postoperatively.14
Management
Classification
Vancouver classification of postoperative periprosthetic femur fractures (Figure 1)
Type A: fracture in the trochanteric region
Type AG (greater trochanter)
Protected–weight bearing
Type AL (lesser trochanter)
Protected–weight bearing
Type B: fracture located around or just distal to the femoral stem.
Type B1 (well-fixed stem)
Management via ORIF affords optimal reduction and stability, promotes healing, and
ultimately leads to rapid mobilization.

augment fixation.
Type B2 (loose stem, good proximal bone stock)
Removal of loose device, cement, and biomembrane should be performed before
reconstruction.
Long-stem revision components to achieve stable distal fixation
During reconstruction, care must be taken to avoid fracture propagation and subsidence.
Type B3 (loose stem, poor proximal bone stock)


Classification
The Vancouver classification is the most widely used classification system and uses
location, component stability, and bone stock to aid in the diagnoses and management
of periprosthetic femur fractures. This classification system is simple, reproducible, and
has been validated. It also provides useful guidelines for management.14
These fractures are managed via protected–weight bearing, specifically limited active
abduction and passive adduction; however, open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
may be considered if the fracture is displaced more than 2.5 cm or if pain, instability, or
abductor weakness is present in patients with a nonunion.14
Fractures of the lesser trochanter primarily are managed via protected–weight bearing,
even if the fracture is displaced. Surgical management may be considered only if a large
portion of the medial cortex is attached.14 If the component is well fixed and the stem
has not subsided, Vancouver type A fractures can heal with nonsurgical management.
Serial radiographs should be carefully scrutinized for stable positioning of the femoral
stem (Figure 2).

Although ORIF affords direct visualization and reduction, extensive soft-tissue dissection
often is required and must be minimized. Minimally invasive plates have become
popular in patients with good bone stock to minimize soft-tissue trauma; however,
limitations include indirect fracture reduction and limited visualization.16
Locking plate constructs also may be advantageous in osteoporotic bone. The plate
should allow for as much overlap as possible and should bypass the implant by at least
six screws.13 For added fixation, cables may be incorporated into the plate construct,
and in patients with poor bone stock or potential stress risers, cortical strut grafts may
augment fixation with dependable biologic union.17
Determining whether a fracture is type B1 or type B2 is critical but may be a challenge.
Although continuous lucency around an implant or a cement mantle fracture may
suggest a loose implant, evidence of loosening may not be revealed until an
intraoperative assessment is performed.16 Therefore, all implants and instrumentation
must be available.
Management of these fractures focuses on fixation past the fracture site. This can be
accomplished via multiple modalities. Extensively porous-coated stems achieve optimal
stability with 4 to 6 cm of interference fit; however, bowed stems may be necessary to
bypass lengths greater than 8 inches. Modular, fluted tapered stems have become more
popular and allow for independent control of anteversion, length, and offset. These
stems may achieve stability within the diaphysis with less than 4 cm of interference fit
through splines, which also provide rotational stability.15
Whether the fracture is reduced first or the femur is reconstructed first largely depends
on fracture morphology and the components used. Prophylactic cables should be placed
distal to the fracture to prevent propagation before preparation of the final stem. Under-
sizing is a common problem that may lead to subsidence. Cortical strut grafts should be
considered to improve stability and enhance bone stock, especially along the tension
surfaces of the femur. Cortical strut grafts have demonstrated reliable outcomes with
good long-term union rates14,18,19 (Figure 3). Modern locking plates also can be used to
supplement fixation.

An allograft prosthetic composite should be considered in young patients to help
augment bone stock. This involves cementing the proximal aspect of a long stem into an
allograft, which is then impacted into the distal femur. The residual bone may be
wrapped around the construct and secured with the use of cables as a form of
vascularized autograft; however, this technique is falling out of favor. Over time, the
allograft may resorb and ultimately result in a weaker construct.14,15
With advancements in technology, proximal femur replacements have become a viable
option to manage Vancouver type B3 fractures. After the prosthesis is removed, the
femur is cut transversely. The stem is then cemented or press-fit into the canal.
Anteversion may be adjusted based on the orientation of the implant, and modular body
segments provide options to adjust fit and control offset. These implants have

These fractures are located well below the femoral stem and may be managed via
constructs such as a blade plate, condylar screw plate, or locking supracondylar plate.
Screw placement may be difficult around a stem, in which case cerclage wires or, if
possible, unicortical locking screws may be used to secure the plate.14 The plate and
stem are overlapped to avoid creating a stress riser. In patients with an ipsilateral total
knee arthroplasty implant, a locked plate should span the THA and total knee
arthroplasty femoral stems16 (Figure 5). Historically, high failure rates resulted from
challenges in achieving sufficient proximal fixation about the implant.

Outcomes
Mortality from periprosthetic femur fractures within the first week is approximately
1%, followed by a 1-year mortality rate of 11% and a cumulative mortality rate of
21%.4,8
Revision surgery may be performed for various reasons, including loosening,
instability, nonunion, infection, and refracture. Although the rates of each of these
complications vary substantially based on patient factors, fracture morphology, and
surgical fixation, generally, revision surgery rates within the first year are
approximately 10% and at 2 years are just over 20%.5,21
Monoblock or modular, fluted, tapered titanium stems often are used to manage
Vancouver type B2 and type B3 periprosthetic fractures because of their ability to
achieve axial and rotational control in the diaphysis distal to the fracture or area of
bone loss. Typically, 4 cm of diaphyseal bone was necessary for distal fixation for fully
coated cylindrical revision stems; however, with newer fluted, tapered titanium stems,
distal fixation can be achieved in as little as 2 cm of diaphyseal bone. Although stem
subsidence is a concern with all revision hip stems, studies have demonstrated an
increase in implant stability, maintenance or improvement of bone stock, and a union
rate higher than 90%.22-24
Rehabilitation
Postoperative management should be tailored to patient characteristics and the
stability of the construct.
Toe-touch weight bearing or protected–weight bearing with limited abduction often is
recommended for 4 to 6 weeks and as long as 12 weeks until definitive healing has

Postoperative Periprosthetic Acetabulum Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Reconstruction of an acetabular fracture around a THA implant may pose a difficult challenge.
Fracture morphology must be analyzed because treatment is based on the injury pattern and
patient characteristics to optimize healing.
Epidemiology
Postoperative periprosthetic acetabulum fractures are rare.

Epidemiology
The incidence of periprosthetic acetabulum fracture occurring during primary THA with
the use of cemented acetabular components is 0.2%; the rate of periprosthetic fracture
with noncemented acetabular components is slightly higher (0.4%).14
Mechanism of Injury
Intraoperative fractures typically occur during cup impaction.
Postoperative acetabulum fractures typically result from high-energy trauma; however, they
also may result from low-energy trauma in patients with osteoporotic bone.26

Mechanism of Injury

These occur especially in older patients or those with poor bone quality.14 Occult
fractures may occur intraoperatively but may not be detected on standard postoperative
radiographs.25 The bone quality along the superolateral wall usually is dense and
sclerotic; therefore, mechanical stress concentrates at this area during cup impaction
and is the most common location of occult periprosthetic fractures.25
Postoperative Risk Factors
Trauma
Osteolysis
Osteopenia or osteoporosis
Abnormal bone quality
Under-reaming or oversizing
Revision surgery

Postoperative Risk factors
Processes that affect the character of host bone may increase the risk of periprosthetic
fracture. For example, the bone stock in a patient with Paget disease is associated with
an increased likelihood of periprosthetic fracture because of sclerotic, unyielding bone.25
In addition, inflammatory arthropathies, such as rheumatoid arthritis, may compromise
the biomechanical quality of bone and, therefore, increase the risk of fracture.27,28
If noncemented press-fit or self-locking cups are inserted, they often are under-reamed
to ensure a good press-fit; however, if a cup is under-reamed by 2 to 4 mm, an increased
risk of periprosthetic occult fracture exists.29
Revision surgery often is associated with bone loss and acetabular osteopenia secondary
to stress shielding. Periprosthetic fractures may occur postoperatively through these

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Postoperative fracture should be suspected if groin pain is present after trauma.
Soft tissue, including prior incisions and abductor function, should be evaluated.
Neurovascular Examination
Vascular injury

Neurovascular Examination
Although vascular injury may occur while securing an acetabular component via screw
placement, the risk of vascular injury remains throughout the life of the prosthesis.
Additional pelvic trauma that leads to an acetabular fracture around a THA prosthesis
mandates thorough and vigilant vascular assessment as part of the initial evaluation.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Judet views: obturator and iliac oblique views
False-profile views
Plain radiographs may underestimate bone loss.
The fracture line may be obscured by metallic components.


Judet views may be obtained by internally and externally rotating the x-ray beam 45°,
which may help identify an anterior or posterior column fracture.28
False-profile radiographs are obtained by positioning a patient’s affected hip and foot
parallel against the cassette with the pelvis rotated 65° toward the x-ray beam.30 These
views help characterize the structural anatomy of the acetabulum and are more
sensitive in detecting pelvic discontinuity.31
Advanced Imaging Studies
CT may help visualize fracture patterns and identify occult fractures.

Advanced Imaging Studies
Advances in CT allow for better metal suppression, which ultimately aids in identifying
occult fractures and complex fracture patterns to aid in surgical planning.28 Occult
fractures may not be detected intraoperatively and also may be undetected on
postoperative radiographs.
Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy also may help identify late fractures.

Bone Scintigraphy
If fractures are suspected and not identified on plain radiographs, bone scintigraphy
may be performed to identify fractures late in the postoperative course. Bone scans may
show increased uptake, even in the absence of fracture, for as long as 2 years
postoperatively.14

Management
Surgical Principles
Bicolumnar fit to support an acetabular implant
Adequate bone stock to secure component

Surgical Principles
Regardless whether periprosthetic acetabulum fractures are managed nonsurgically or
surgically or whether they occur intraoperatively or postoperatively, security of the
implant and the construct is gauged by the fit between the anterior and posterior
column.
Bone stock plays a vital role in securing an acetabular cup and must be assessed in the
management of these injuries to help guide implant selection and construct design. If
possible, defects should be filled with bone graft to aid in fixation. Conversely, poor bone
stock often requires additional fixation and support via augments and larger constructs.
Classification
Paprosky classification of periprosthetic fractures of the acetabulum

Classification
The Paprosky classification of periprosthetic fractures of the acetabulum (Table 1)
categorizes the wide array of patterns of periprosthetic fractures of the acetabulum and
helps guide management.28 The classification system uses variables such as timing,
mechanism of injury, bone loss, and stability.32

Intraoperative Fractures
Type I fractures may be further distinguished based on displacement. Stable,
nondisplaced fractures (type IA) typically are stabilized with the use of
supplemental screws through the cup and with postoperative weight-bearing
restrictions.14,32 Conversely, displaced, unstable fractures (type IB) require

should be reduced and fixed; for example, if the posterior column is involved, it
may be fixed with the use of a posterior column plate.14,28 The acetabulum
should be re-reamed, and the cup should be impacted back into position; if
insufficient bone stock is presents, augments or bone graft should be
considered.28 Type I fractures that are not recognized intraoperatively can be
managed as postoperative periprosthetic acetabulum fractures.
During revision surgery, bone loss in inevitable, especially in well-fixed
components. Type II fractures occur as the acetabular cups are removed and
may be categorized as type IIA if less than 50% bone loss is present or type IIB if
more than 50% bone loss is present. The primary goal should be to create a
stable pelvis. This may require single or double plating, screws, bone grafting,
augments, or larger acetabular implants14,28 (Figure 6)

Postoperative Fractures
Traumatic (type III)
Spontaneous (type IV)
Pelvic discontinuity (type V)

Postoperative Fractures
Traumatic fractures can be subdivided into stable (type IIIA) and unstable (type IIIB)
injuries. Type IIIA fractures may be managed nonsurgically via restricted–weight bearing
and activity modifications; however, although these fractures can unite, a strong
possibility exists that they may become unstable and require surgical management.
Therefore, they should be monitored closely via serial radiographs.5,8 Type IIIB fractures
are highly mobile. In addition to removing the hardware, the fractures must be
stabilized.28 Posterior column fractures may be stabilized with the use of a pelvic plate
or screws before acetabular implant insertion, which may be performed with the use of
porous revision implants that are subsequently secured with the use of multiple
screws.14 A multihole acetabular cup with multiple screw fixation on each side of the
fracture is necessary for component stability (Figure 7).

Spontaneous fractures are less common and occur in patients with worsening bone
stock.28 If more than 50% of bone stock is preserved (type IVA), large revision acetabular
cups may be used and secured with the use of multiple implants and bone graft as
necessary.14 Spontaneous fractures with more than 50% of bone loss (type IVB) are
complex problems that should not be managed solely with the use of large cups and
ultimately require additional reconstruction. Although plates and screws may be
necessary to restore column stability, metallic augments often are used to manage the
bony defects; however, if host bone is insufficient to support bony ingrowth, cages and
cup-cage constructs may be used.
Pelvic discontinuity, defined by the separation of the ilium from the ischiopubic segment,
is a challenging complication that may occur because of a periprosthetic acetabulum
fracture. Successful management of pelvic discontinuity depends on not only host bone
stock but also the potential for healing and bony ingrowth to achieve rigid, durable
fixation. If more than 50% bone stock remains (type VA), posterior column compression
plating before cup insertion helps stabilize the discontinuity and promote fracture
healing.33 Highly porous, flexible cups have a higher coefficient of friction that leads to
improved osseointegration and biomechanical stability via improved load transfer and
often are used in these settings.34 These cups may be secured with the use of screws
and should have at least 50% contact with host bone.14,33 They may be especially
advantageous if bone quality is compromised via pelvic irradiation (type VC).33,35
If less than 50% bone stock remains (type VB), constructs that span the discontinuity may
be required to manage the defect. A cup-cage construct uses a jumbo acetabular cup
(>62 to 55 mm) on the remaining host bone, and to fill any remaining bony defects,
highly porous metal augments may be secured to the bone with the use of screws and
subsequently cemented to the cup. A cage is then placed over the component to span
the discontinuity from the ilium to the ischium; however, cup-cage constructs are
associated with high failure rates in patients with pelvic discontinuity.33 Custom triflange
components also may be used in complex cases of pelvic discontinuity. CT scans can be
used to create a three-dimensional model for which three flanges extending to the ilium,
ischium, and pubis are then designed to secure the component into place.33 Cancellous
screws are then used to compress the implant to the bone along the ischium and the

The preference of the authors of this lesson is to use acetabular distraction with porous
metal augments. A laminar spreader is placed between the augment and the posterior
column to distract the discontinuity, and reaming is sequentially performed to achieve a
press-fit with a cup approximately 4 to 8 mm larger than the original defect. The porous
shell is impacted, and the laminar spreader is removed, providing compression of the
columns onto the cup. Screws are used on both sides of the defect. The porous cup acts
as an internal plate to achieve biologic fixation on the anterior and posterior columns

Complications
Dislocation
Infection
Sciatic nerve injury

Complications
Dislocation remains a common complication that is a direct result of surgical exposure
and fracture fixation. Large extensile approaches often are necessary to reduce the
fracture and place implants; with these approaches, abductor weakness remains a
problem and may lead to a higher risk of dislocation (as high as 40% to 50% in patients
with pelvic discontinuity).33,36 Larger femoral heads may be used to minimize this risk,
and although constrained liners also may be used, they may place additional stress
along the bone-implant interface if bone stock is compromised.
An increased risk of prosthetic joint infection exists, which likely is a result of increased
surgical time, multiple prior surgical procedure, and large extensile exposures to reduce
the fracture and place implants that may devascularize tissue.33,36
The posterolateral approach affords excellent exposure to the acetabulum; however, the
sciatic nerve must be identified during this approach. The nerve may be scarred down in
patients with severe discontinuity or in patients who have undergone multiple revision
procedures and may be inadvertently injured during the approach or with retractor
placement. Ischial dissection during the placement of a cage or securing a flange also
places the sciatic nerve at risk for injury.34

Rehabilitation
Postoperative management should be tailored to patient characteristics and the stability of the
construct.
Protected–weight bearing for 6 to 12 weeks

Rehabilitation
Patients who undergo nonsurgical treatment for a periprosthetic acetabulum fracture
often are treated via weight-bearing restrictions; however, given the complex nature of
some of these constructs, postoperative weight-bearing restrictions also may help
protect the construct and promote osseointegration and healing.
